ON FLUIDITY

We have distinguished between the two cases just mentioned because, in those, we assume that certain adventitious corpuscles remain within the body, contributing to its firmness and entering into its constitution—even if perhaps only in a small quantity. Here, however, we assume that these agents, without materially contributing to the composition of the body upon which they act, merely agitate and variously move the particles that compose it, perhaps by breaking some, bending and entangling others, and, in a word, so changing the texture that those parts which previously either moved separately or adhered less strictly are now reduced to a tighter space or a more intricate texture, and by this means are more firmly connected to one another. It is evident, both in certain examples already mentioned and in willow rods, that the mere arrangement of the parts of a body as they relate to one another, with no added extrinsic material, can contribute greatly to stability. Willow rods, when loose and lying in a pile, can easily be separated from one another, but when woven into a basket, they cohere so firmly that if one is lifted, all the others are raised with it.
